title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
hook: RL post-training is usually studied apart from pretraining. Using chess as a testbed, this paper shows post-RL performance is predictable from pretraining loss alone.
key_points: Uses chess as a controlled testbed: pretrain 5M-1B parameter models on human games, SFT on synthetic reasoning traces, then RL on puzzles with verifiable rewards.
Post-RL performance at a given RL compute level is well-predicted from pretraining loss alone.
The slope of the RL reward curve improves roughly linearly with pretraining tokens seen.
RL doesn't just sharpen the SFT policy uniformly: on easy puzzles it amplifies moves SFT already preferred; on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves nearly absent under SFT.
The same predictive pattern (longer pretraining -> higher, faster post-RL gains) replicates when transferring to a 1B math-domain language model.
content_html: RL post-training gets most of the credit for today's reasoning models, but it's almost always studied disconnected from the pretraining that comes before it. This paper asks: what does pretraining actually buy you when RL comes next — and what does RL actually change?
extra_html:
Jingyan Shen, Pavel Izmailov, and colleagues sidestep the usual problem — pretraining corpora are too vast and uncontrolled to cleanly attribute behavior — by using chess as a testbed. They pretrain models from 5M to 1B parameters on human chess games, run supervised fine-tuning on synthetic reasoning traces, then apply RL on chess puzzles with verifiable rewards, mirroring the standard LLM pipeline end to end. They find post-RL performance at a fixed RL compute budget is well-predicted just from pretraining loss, and that the RL reward curve's slope improves roughly linearly with pretraining tokens seen.

Beyond scaling curves, they find RL isn't a uniform sharpening of the SFT policy: on easy puzzles it mostly amplifies moves the SFT policy already leaned toward, while on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves that were nearly absent beforehand. To check this isn't a chess-only artifact, they retrain a 1B model on math-domain text and see the same pattern: longer pretraining leads to higher and faster post-RL gains. The result is a quantitative account of the pretraining-to-RL interface, plus a reusable controlled testbed for studying it further. arXiv, July 2026.

related.title: Chinchilla: Compute-Optimal Scaling
related.hook: Most giant models were starved of data. Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget you should grow parameters and tokens together — and a smaller, longer-trained model won.

related.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
related.hook: GRPO dropped the value network from PPO and scored each answer against a group of sampled siblings — the cheap RL recipe that made DeepSeek-R1's reasoning trainable.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors use chess instead of standard LLM pretraining corpora to study RL's returns?
flashcards.back_html: Standard corpora are vast and uncontrolled, making it hard to attribute behavior to pretraining vs. RL, and compute sweeps across both stages are prohibitively expensive. Chess gives a controlled testbed.

flashcards.prompt: What predicts post-RL performance at a given RL compute level, per this paper?

choices.text: Only the number of RL steps, independent of pretraining
The size of the SFT dataset alone

flashcards.explanation_html: They find post-RL performance at a given RL compute level is well-predicted from pretraining loss, and the RL reward curve's slope scales roughly linearly with pretraining tokens.

flashcards.prompt: How does RL affect easy puzzles differently from hard puzzles, according to the paper?
flashcards.back_html: On easy puzzles it amplifies correct moves the SFT policy already favored; on hard puzzles it surfaces correct moves that were nearly absent under SFT.

flashcards.prompt: Did the chess-derived findings hold up outside chess?

choices.text: Yes — a 1B math-domain model showed the same pattern: longer pretraining, higher and faster post-RL gains
No — the pattern was specific to chess and did not transfer
It was only tested on chess, with no transfer experiment

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors trained a 1B model on math-domain text and found the same predictive pattern emerged there too.
